cells.tense: Something is ending right now and you're not arguing with it — you're here, at the threshold, letting the ending finish and watching what walks in.
cells.ask: Pick one thing that's closing and name out loud what it settled, then let it stay closed today — a clear line where the muddle was.
cells.core:
You can hold an ending without either rushing it or refusing it. What's finishing gets finished, and what's arriving gets met — you don't need the next thing to be certain before you can let the last thing go. That's why the room you're in doesn't feel like wreckage.

The harder part is that an ending you've honored still asks something of you afterward — a fair split of what was shared, a clean handoff, a plain accounting of what you gave and what you got. Letting things be finished is not the same as letting them stay unsettled. Offer one of those loose counters something honest today: one thing you've been carrying unevenly, set down where it belongs, in words that balance without scorekeeping.
cells.sheetLine: You let the finished thing finish, and you're still here for what's next.
cells.verb: letting what's finished be finished so what's arriving can land
cells.place: at the threshold, where what's been outside is entering now

cells.tense: You're several endings ahead of yourself — braced for what hasn't arrived, clearing rooms before anyone has left them.
cells.ask: Let one thing go untended for a day and stay with someone while it's still unfinished — being with it instead of ahead of it.
cells.core:
You can end things. That's not in doubt — when something is done you know it and you act. The muscle works.

What's also true is that the ending keeps arriving before the living does, and the name you give it — freedom, a fresh start — sits on top of a bracing that hasn't stopped. Staying near one unfinished thing without resolving it, without being the one who decides how it goes, is the harder and more useful move. Let someone else's read on what's happening sit alongside yours for a day. You don't have to merge with it — just not close it from a distance before it has a chance to speak.
cells.sheetLine: You're ending things before they've had a chance to live.
cells.verb: letting what's finished be finished so what's arriving can land
cells.place: at the threshold, where what's been outside is entering now

cells.tense: Something already closed behind you and you're still standing at it, holding the door, calling it loyalty.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you're keeping that's already finished, and put a date on when you'll let it go — the first move of something you actually want.
cells.core:
You can love a thing and still know it's done — the same care pointed in a different direction. At its steady hour this looks like someone who walked through and remembers it warmly, who can say 'that was good and it's over' without the word over doing any damage. The keeping isn't the problem; the keeping when the thing has already gone is.

What's stuck is that holding the finished thing close feels like keeping faith with something. But the faith isn't in the object — it's yours, and it doesn't need the object to survive. Trying harder at what's already stopped doesn't loosen it. What moves it is wanting something enough to go get it — a direction, however small, that you chose this week, not one that arrived. Pick one thing you'd actually like to happen and take a first step toward it today. Movement from a real want is what unsticks the door.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping faith with something that's already finished.
cells.verb: letting what's finished be finished so what's arriving can land
cells.place: at the threshold, where what's been outside is entering now

cells.tense: Something is ending in you right now and it hasn't been named — you're still writing in this room as if nothing is closing.
cells.ask: Write the sentence 'this is finished' about one thing on a piece of paper, then say aloud what comes next in it — you deciding, not the situation.
cells.core:
Structure is something you do well — things make sense when you're the one holding the shape, and people lean on that. That's not a small thing; it's most of why the room stays calm.

Something is finishing here and it hasn't been given a name, so it's happening without a vote from you. The way it comes back into your hands is simpler than the situation makes it look: say what's ended, in your own voice, and organize what comes next instead of letting it organize you. Naming one finished thing and one next step isn't a big move — it's the smaller one underneath everything you've been managing. That's what puts the pen back in your hand without needing to make a scene of it.
cells.sheetLine: Something is ending in you and you haven't said so yet.
cells.verb: letting what's finished be finished so what's arriving can land
cells.place: at the threshold, where what's been outside is entering now

attempts.check: The record licenses the card's mechanism and the seat's location, not any scene or history — so no cell may say what ended, who left, how long ago, or what the person felt about it. A reader might reasonably object that 'what's ending in you' is a large claim about their private life; each cell therefore names the capacity's pattern as a possibility and keeps the ending unspecified. The asks are acts anyone can do today regardless of whether the read is right — write what's finished on paper, let one thing go untended, put a date on one thing, leave it unanswered — and each teaches something even if the read is wrong. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader would be any line that congratulates the tense ('you're right on time'), which is cut everywhere.
